cases.title: Splenic artery aneurysm
cases.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a 28-mm saccular splenic artery aneurysm with documented interval growth and wishes to become pregnant.

questions.question: Which feature most strongly supports treatment rather than observation?
options: Interval growth, relevant size and planned pregnancy
Age below 40 years as the only factor
questions.explanation: Growth, aneurysm size and pregnancy-related rupture risk are important factors when considering treatment.

questions.question: For a distal aneurysm in a tortuous splenic artery, which endovascular strategy is commonly used when anatomy is suitable?
options: Selective embolisation that excludes inflow and outflow to the aneurysm
questions.explanation: Isolation of the aneurysm by occluding inflow and outflow can prevent antegrade and retrograde reperfusion.

questions.question: Which complication should be considered after splenic artery embolisation?
questions.explanation: The extent of splenic ischaemia depends on embolisation level and preserved collateral supply.

questions.question: What is the desired completion angiographic result?
options: Persistent filling of the aneurysm sac
Exclusion of the aneurysm while preserving viable splenic perfusion when possible
Occlusion of the common hepatic artery
questions.explanation: The aim is durable aneurysm exclusion while limiting unnecessary splenic ischaemia.

cases.title: TACE for hepatocellular carcinoma
cases.stem: A cirrhotic patient has multifocal HCC confined to the liver, preserved liver function and no macroscopic vascular invasion.

questions.question: What is the basic therapeutic principle of transarterial chemoembolisation?
options: Deliver therapy through tumour-feeding arteries and reduce tumour perfusion by embolisation
questions.explanation: TACE combines selective intra-arterial treatment with embolisation of tumour arterial supply.

questions.question: Which angiographic information is essential before embolic delivery?
options: Tumour arterial supply and branches at risk of non-target embolisation
Only the inferior vena cava anatomy
questions.explanation: Detailed arterial mapping allows selective treatment and avoidance of extrahepatic non-target embolisation.

questions.question: Which finding should prompt reassessment before proceeding with embolisation?
options: Unprotected flow to a relevant extrahepatic branch
questions.explanation: Unprotected extrahepatic flow increases the risk of gastrointestinal or other non-target injury.

questions.question: After locoregional treatment of HCC, response assessment should focus particularly on:
options: Residual viable enhancing tumour rather than size change alone
questions.explanation: Viable enhancing tumour is central to response assessment after embolisation-based therapy.

questions.question: The objective of percutaneous varicocele embolisation is to:
options: Occlude incompetent gonadal venous pathways and relevant collaterals
questions.explanation: Treatment aims to eliminate pathological reflux while preserving non-target venous drainage.

questions.question: For symptomatic central venous stenosis associated with a haemodialysis access, the usual first endovascular treatment is:
questions.explanation: Angioplasty is commonly first-line; stents are reserved for selected recoil, rupture or recurrent lesions.

questions.question: During radiologically inserted gastrostomy, an important safety step is to:
options: Confirm gastric position and exclude interposed colon before puncture
questions.explanation: Appropriate gastric distension and imaging reduce the risk of transcolonic access.

questions.question: Why is detailed pelvic arterial anatomy crucial during prostatic artery embolisation?
options: Anastomoses may communicate with vesical, rectal and penile territories
The prostate has no arterial supply
The prostate is supplied only by the thoracic aorta
questions.explanation: Variable pelvic anastomoses create the principal risk of non-target embolisation.

questions.question: When treating a visceral artery pseudoaneurysm with significant collateral supply, which principle is useful?
options: Exclude both inflow and outflow when feasible
Use anticoagulation alone in every case
questions.explanation: Sandwich/isolation techniques can prevent retrograde filling through collateral pathways.

questions.question: Which technique reduces patient radiation dose during fluoroscopy?
options: Tight collimation and an appropriate low pulse rate
Keeping the field of view maximally open
questions.explanation: Collimation and reduced pulse rate are effective dose-optimisation measures.

questions.question: For a long-term tunnelled central venous catheter, the tip is generally positioned:
options: In an appropriate central venous location, commonly near the cavoatrial junction depending on device and indication
In the distal femoral vein in every case
questions.explanation: Appropriate central tip location is required for reliable high-flow access and to reduce complications.

questions.question: If non-target embolisation is suspected during an injection, the immediate response should be to:
options: Stop the injection, reassess the vascular anatomy and reposition if appropriate
questions.explanation: Stopping delivery and reassessing anatomy is the first step to limit further non-target injury.
